key_cases.case_name: Union Leader Corp. v. N.H. Dep't of Safety
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the dismissal of a Right-to-Know suit for State Police records of the response to the Sununu Youth Services Center, clarifying that juvenile confidentiality under RSA 169-B:35 reaches records held by non-court agencies only to the extent disclosure would run counter to the purpose of rehabilitating delinquent minors, and remanded for that determination and for consideration of redaction.
key_cases.relevance: Public and press access to records of the State's response at a youth facility is the practical mechanism by which systemic problems in state custody are surfaced.
key_cases.quote: This refinement effectuates the juvenile delinquency statutes’ purpose of rehabilitating delinquent minors while also ensuring “the greatest possible public access to the actions, discussions and records of all public bodies.”

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a child protection agency's failure to remove a child from an abusive parent, despite repeated reports and its own suspicions, did not deprive the child of liberty without due process, because the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on the State to protect against private violence absent a custodial relationship.
key_cases.relevance: Oversight findings that an agency failed to act do not by themselves generate a federal constitutional claim, which is why administrative and legislative review carries the burden.
key_cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the 'reasonable efforts' requirement of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), does not create a right enforceable by beneficiaries either through 42 U.S.C. § 1983 or by implied private right of action.
key_cases.relevance: Federal oversight of state child welfare performance operates through the Secretary's plan-approval and funding levers rather than through private suits.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents

mandatory_reporters: Any person (universal mandatory reporting) — N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 169-C:29
Physicians, surgeons, county medical examiners, psychiatrists, residents, interns
Registered nurses and hospital personnel (admission, examination, care and treatment)
Teachers, school officials, school nurses, school counselors
Social workers, day care workers, and any other child or foster care workers
reporting_details: New Hampshire is a universal-reporter state: RSA 169-C:29 lists physicians, dentists, psychologists, registered nurses and hospital personnel, teachers, school officials and school nurses, social workers, day care and other child or foster care workers, law enforcement officials and clergy, and closes with “any other person having reason to suspect that a child has been abused or neglected,” all of whom “shall report the same in accordance with this chapter.” RSA 169-C:30 sets the route and the form: an oral report “shall be made immediately by telephone or otherwise, and followed within 48 hours by a report in writing, if so requested, to the department” — the Department of Health and Human Services, which takes reports through the DCYF Central Intake Unit at 603-271-6562 or 1-800-894-5533 (in-state only), staffed 24 hours a day including weekends and holidays.
